doc.title: Jerry Bergonzi interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 7, 2022

title: Originators versus copycats; Billy Mitchell and Sweets Edison quotes
summary: Responding to quotes from Mitchell and Edison, he talks about souls arriving with emotional baggage and how everyone borrows from predecessors before finding their own sound.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I want to read — I know there’s a discussion that happens about original sound etcetera. I want to read two very short quotes from — this is the generation before you and I. This is from Billy Mitchell. He said “There’s a lot of youngsters get caught up in the proficiency and the musicality and they forget the emotion. The emotion takes longer. You have to experience it.” And from Harry “Sweets” Edison, “Our ambition in my day not to be an imitator but an originator, and they used to say they’d rather be the world’s worst originator than the world’s greatest imitator. Nowadays it seems like musicians have their idols and they don’t venture anyplace else but what their idol is playing.” Do you have any comment?
I agree with both of those things but in one — the first one was Billy Taylor you said?

Billy Mitchell, sorry, yup. Billy Mitchell. The first thing I would say was that sometimes people when they come into this life they come in with heavy baggage. So they don’t even need to experience a lot of emotional stuff, they already have it, depending on their upbringing. They have their mother and father were fighting all the time or they were in a poverty situation. So their experience, their soul is already, you know they say the soul picks the lifetime, right? So I don’t necessarily think that you need to get your life experience to the life you’re living, you already have it, even though you’re getting it in this life, you already came in with something.
And the other thing is would I rather be the worst…

…originator than a really good copy cat. That’s a fantastic thing because in today’s world nobody learns how to play by walking out of a cave one day and they learn how to play. You have to know the history of this. You listen to early John Coltrane you can hear Dexter Gordon in it, you can hear Sonny Rollins in it, you can hear Jimmy Heath, you can hear of course Charlie Parker in everybody. But you know etcetera, etcetera. And then you can hear later Dexter and there’s some Coltrane things in there you know. So nobody — you know you hear Sonny — Joe Henderson’s got some Sonny Rollins in

there for sure and Newk that he tips his hat to. And early Sonny Rollins if there’s no Charlie Parker there’s no Sonny Rollins. Just the language. So everybody’s getting something from somebody. At a certain point you say I breathe I’m valid. I’m going to listen to myself and try to do, get my sound — you don’t even have to try. You can’t get away from your sound even if you try to sound like somebody else you’re just going to end up sounding like you trying to sound like somebody else. So you say yeah, I’m going to be more me. And believe in yourself. I tell my students if I could tell you one thing believe in yourself. You are valid.
